questions.question: A single-server queue has arrival rate $\lambda$, mean inter-arrival time $\mathbb{E}[X]$, mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$, service rate $\mu=1/\mathbb{E}[S]$ and departure rate $\delta$. Which pair of expressions both equal the server load $\rho$ in every such queue, whether or not it is rate stable?
For a single-server queue with arrival rate $\lambda$ and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$, what does the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ measure?
options: The offered work per unit time, in units of the capacity of the server.
The long-run fraction of time during which the server is busy.
The long-run number of jobs that complete service per unit time.
The probability that an arriving job finds the server busy.

questions.question: For a single-server queue with arrival rate $\lambda$, departure rate $\delta$ and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$, compare the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ with the utilization $\delta\mathbb{E}[S]$. Which statement about their possible values is correct?
options: Both the load and the utilization are always at most $1$.
The load is at most $1$, but the utilization can exceed $1$.
Both can exceed $1$ when jobs arrive faster than they are served.
The load can exceed $1$, while the utilization is at most $1$.

questions.question: In a $G^B/G^C/c$ station, batches arrive at rate $\lambda$ with mean size $\mathbb{E}[B]$, each job needs mean service $\mathbb{E}[S]$, and each of $c$ servers serves on average $\mathbb{E}[C]$ jobs per service time. Which single change, all else fixed, increases the load $\rho$?
options: Adding a server, so that $c$ increases.
A longer mean time between batch arrivals.

questions.question: Two single-server stations have the same arrival rate $\lambda$ and the same mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$. At station A every service takes exactly $\mathbb{E}[S]$; at station B service times vary widely. How do their loads compare?
options: Station B has the larger load, because its widely varying service times bring more work per job.
Station A has the larger load, because at B the short jobs free capacity that offsets the long ones.
Both stations have the same load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, because the load depends on the service times only through their mean.
Station B has the larger load only when $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ is close to $1$.

questions.question: Customers arrive at a single counter at rate $\lambda=18$ per hour and each service takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=3$ minutes. What is the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$?
At a single server the mean time between consecutive arrivals is $\mathbb{E}[X]=8$ minutes and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=6$ minutes. What is the load $\rho$?
A call centre with $c=5$ identical agents receives $\lambda=30$ calls per hour; each call takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=6$ minutes. What is the load $\rho$ per agent?
Jobs arrive at a single server at times $1,2,6,7,11,12,\dots$ (two arrivals in every block of $5$ time units), and each job needs exactly $2$ time units of service. What is the load $\rho$?
In a discrete-time queue the number of arrivals per day has mean $\lambda=9$ and the daily capacity has mean $\mu=10$. What are the load $\rho$ and the drift of the queue length?

In a single-server queue with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$, the long-run arrival rate $\lambda$ equals the long-run departure rate $\delta$. Which conclusion about the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ is justified?
options: $\rho=1$, since jobs leave exactly as fast as they arrive.
$\rho<1$ strictly, since a queue with $\rho=1$ never has $\lambda=\delta$.
$\rho\le1$, but $\rho$ may differ from the utilization $\delta\mathbb{E}[S]$.

questions.question: Two separate stations each receive jobs at rate $\lambda$. Station A has one server with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]/2$. Station B has $c=2$ identical servers, each with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$. How do the loads of A and B compare?
options: B has load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, twice that of A, as each server faces all arrivals.
B has load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]/4$, half that of A, as arrivals and capacity are both split.
A has load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, twice that of B, as faster service brings no less work.

questions.question: A single-server queue never blocks jobs, and its arrival rate exceeds its service rate, $\lambda>\mu$, so $\rho>1$. Which statement describes the long-run departure rate $\delta$ and the queue?
options: Every job is eventually served, so $\delta=\lambda$ and the queue is rate stable.
The server is always busy, so $\delta=\mu$ and the queue length stays bounded.
Jobs leave at rate $\delta=\lambda-\mu$, the excess of arrivals over capacity.
The queue grows without bound and $\delta=\mu<\lambda$.

questions.question: Parties of on average $\mathbb{E}[B]=2$ visitors arrive at a boat tour at $\lambda=20$ parties per hour. There are $c=3$ boats; each trip takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=15$ minutes and carries on average $\mathbb{E}[C]=5$ visitors. What is the load $\rho$?

Requests arrive at $\lambda=50$ per hour at a pool of identical clerks, and each request takes on average $\mathbb{E}[S]=9$ minutes. Management wants the load per clerk $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]/c$ to be at most $0.8$. What is the smallest number of clerks $c$?

Jobs are offered to a single server at $\lambda=10$ per hour with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.15$ hours. A job that finds the server busy is rejected, and in the long run $60\%$ of the offered jobs are rejected. What is the load $\rho$?

Let $A(t)$ count the arrivals at a single server in $[0,t]$, and let $S_k$ be the service time of job $k$. Which assumption does the argument $\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=1}^{A(t)}S_k\to\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ as $t\to\infty$, with $\lambda>0$, rely on?
options: The service times $S_k$ are independent of the times at which the jobs arrive.
The arrival process is Poisson, so that $A(t)/t$ converges to $\lambda$.
The load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ is below $1$, so the server keeps up.

questions.question: A single server with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ is busy $90\%$ of the time in the long run, so its utilization $\delta\mathbb{E}[S]$ is $0.9$. It is unknown whether arriving jobs are ever blocked. What can be concluded about the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: $\rho=0.9$, because load and utilization are the same quantity.
$\rho\le0.9$, because the utilization is an upper bound for the load.
$\rho\ge0.9$, and $\rho$ may even exceed $1$, because jobs cannot depart faster than they are offered.
$\rho<1$, because a busy fraction below $1$ shows the server keeps up.

questions.question: A single server handles two job classes. Class 1 jobs arrive at $4$ per hour and need on average $6$ minutes; class 2 jobs arrive at $2$ per hour and need on average $15$ minutes. What is the server load $\rho$?

A clinic's weekly intake capacity follows a repeating $5$-week cycle: $14$ intakes in each of $4$ weeks and $9$ in the holiday week. On average $12$ patients per week need an intake. What is the load $\rho$?
